newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Centam workers, rebels criticize gov't on May Day.
newsitem.headline: Centam workers, rebels criticize gov't on May Day.

text.p: Hundreds of former rebels of the Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit (URNG) and thousands of labour unions and leftists elsewhere in Central America took to the streets on Thursday for Labour Day protests of privitization plans.
There were also protests of government policies and marchers demanding higher wages in Central American countries.

Guatemala's URNG was once an illegal organisation in armed rebellion against the state until December when the government and guerrilla leaders signed a historic peace treaty ending 36 years of civil war.
"One people, one party," chanted marching URNG members. The former rebels are forming a legitimate political party.

Labour unions, women's groups, organisations of illegal squatters, street vendors associations and leftist political parties marched through downtown Guatemala City and formed a sea of waving banners before the National Palace.

"State properties belong to the people. We won't allow their privatisation," read one of many banners protesting government plans to sell off the telephone company, railroad, electric plants and other state enterprises.
Workers in El Salvador are asking for a pardon of millions in agriculture debt, a new labour code, higher salaries and stronger education and health programmes.

"This is a protest dedicated to saying no to neo-liberalism," El Salvador telecommunications union director Adilio Mejia told Reuters. Neo-liberalism has caused "greater poverty, unemployment and marginalization," he added.
Honduran workers took up a similar cry on the streets in May Day parades, as workers criticised the government of Carlos Reina for delaying the implementation of fixed prices on certain basic goods.
Costa Rican marches for Labour Day were peaceful and sparse, with about 2,000 people in a parade through the streets in that capital San Jose.
In Nicaragua, Labour Day passed with a specter of its former raucous protests, as just some 5,000 people paraded through Managua.
